items.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 4.2, Canon Layers at Scale where Synthetic Pretraining Resonates in Reality
items.headline: Canon layers at 8B/1T tokens save ~30% of pretraining tokens for equal MMLU; with Canon, gated linear attention matches Gated DeltaNet
items.summary: Tests whether architecture findings from small synthetic 'playgrounds' (<100M params) hold at real scale. Runs 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3B-8B parameters on 1-2T Nemotron-CC tokens (about 100k USD per 8B run). Canon layers add cheap local token mixing between positions inside each block. The paper also introduces GLA5 and GDN2, which add low-rank output gates to gated linear attention and Gated DeltaNet.
items.result: Canon layers save about 30% of pretraining tokens for the same MMLU accuracy at 8B. With Canon, gated linear attention matches Gated DeltaNet and beats Mamba2 at 8B/1T. At 1.3B/100B tokens, carefully tuned architectures differ very little. Even at 8B/1T, linear models that match Transformers on standard benchmarks cannot reliably retrieve from a 500-token context, and no model reliably beats chance on a simple two-hop question.
items.critique: Single-author study whose cost and scale cannot easily be reproduced. The 30% figure is measured on one benchmark (MMLU) at one scale. Per the arXiv comments, results, recipes and code have been public since 9 Dec 2025 (github.com/facebookresearch/PhysicsLM4), so this is a write-up of earlier released work rather than wholly new results. Details here rest on the abstract. Hardware and the full linear-model baselines (e.g., hybrids) are not described there.

items.title: Efficient and Robust Drafting with Multi-Token Prediction
items.headline: G-MTP: multi-token-prediction drafter heads for Gemma 4 report up to 3.1x speculative-decoding speedup (2.3x on small on-device models)
items.summary: Speculative decoding needs a drafter that is cheap but close to the target model. G-MTP extends an existing backbone LLM (tested on the Gemma 4 family) with Multi-Token Prediction drafting. It makes three changes: target activations are injected into the drafter, the drafter cross-attends to the target's KV cache without copying it, and a clustered vocabulary projection cuts output-layer cost. The paper also gives parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes that keep the drafter aligned with the backbone when the backbone is post-trained for new domains.
items.result: Up to 3.1x speedup for large server-side setups and up to 2.3x for smaller models aimed at memory-constrained devices. The fine-tuning recipe needs up to 1.83x fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone.
items.critique: Workshop paper, summarized from the poster page; no arXiv version or code was found. The abstract names no baselines (EAGLE-style, Medusa, or independent draft models), and gives no acceptance rates, model sizes or hardware. 'Up to' figures hide the typical speedup. Gemma 4 only, so how well the method transfers to other model families is untested.

items.title: dLoop: Looped Diffusion Language Models via Recurrent Latent Refinement
items.headline: dLoop converts a pretrained diffusion LM into a Prelude-Loop-Coda model that reruns a shared middle block on the masked state
items.summary: Takes a pretrained diffusion language model and restructures it into Prelude, Loop and Coda stages. A parameter-shared intermediate block is applied repeatedly to the same partially masked state, so latent refinement happens inside one denoising step rather than only across steps. This trades more compute per forward pass for more tokens decoded per pass.
items.result: Highest or tied-highest accuracy on GSM8K, MATH, MBPP and HumanEval among the methods compared. With tokens per forward pass (TPF) adjusted for loop compute, it beats Fast-dLLM on both accuracy and TPF on all four benchmarks and dParallel on three. It is more accurate than d3LLM on all four, but d3LLM has higher TPF.
items.critique: The abstract gives no absolute numbers, base-model size, wall-clock latency or hardware, so how large the gains are is unknown. Only four math and code benchmarks. Loop-adjusted TPF is the authors' own metric, and real latency depends on kernels and batch size. No code link on the abstract page.

items.title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
items.headline: PRKV ranks KV-cache tokens by Personalized PageRank over attention graphs for training-free eviction at up to 90% compression
items.summary: Most KV-cache eviction methods score each token by the attention it receives directly. PRKV instead treats attention as a transition graph between tokens and runs Personalized PageRank on it. This estimates multi-hop, global importance, so tokens that matter only indirectly are kept. It is training-free and evicts the lowest-ranked entries.
items.result: At moderate to aggressive compression ratios, up to 90%, PRKV is competitive with established eviction baselines on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval and chain-of-thought reasoning across several LLM families. It also reduces peak memory with low end-to-end overhead. The abstract gives no accuracy or latency numbers.
items.critique: 'Competitive with' rather than better, and the baselines and models are not named in the abstract. The cost of PageRank iterations per decode step is described only as 'low overhead', with no figures. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 per the comments; no code link on the abstract page.

items.title: A Sparse Low-Rank Biclique Decomposition for Graphs
items.headline: Signed biclique decomposition compresses graph matrices over 10x and speeds SpMM up to 6x vs cuSPARSE on suitable real graphs
items.summary: Represents integer-weighted graph adjacency matrices as a sum of sparse, signed, binary rank-one factors (bicliques) plus a sparse residual. Shared-neighborhood structure is factored out once instead of being stored edge by edge. Sparse-dense matrix multiplication (SpMM), the core kernel of GNNs and graph analytics, then runs on the compact form.
items.result: On real graphs with shared-neighborhood structure, compression factors above 10 and SpMM speedups of up to 6x over cuSPARSE.
items.critique: Gains are stated only for graphs that have the right structure. Graphs without it, and the cost of computing the decomposition, are not quantified in the abstract. 'Up to 6x' gives no median. No end-to-end GNN training or inference timing. Graph kernels, not LLMs. Details rest on the arXiv listing abstract; author list is the first three names shown.

items.title: Forget Freely, Grep Later: Lossless, Index-Free Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.headline: GrepMem keeps a lossless plain-text log and lets an RL-trained Qwen3.5-9B regex-search it, reaching 95-97% on ContextBench
items.summary: Long-horizon agents usually manage context by summarizing or embedding-indexing history, which loses information. GrepMem drops old context from the window but appends it to a plain-text log, and trains the model with RL (Qwen3.5-9B) to retrieve from that log with regex searches. It needs no vector index.
items.result: 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench versus at most 21% for lossy baselines. It beats SUPO's summarization approach by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi.
items.critique: The lossy baselines are weak by construction on a benchmark that tests exact recall, so the 95-97% vs 21% gap partly reflects the benchmark. One 9B model. The latency and token cost of the extra grep tool calls are not reported in the abstract. Details rest on the arXiv listing abstract; author list is the first three names shown.

items.title: LLMs Are Already Confidence-Aware Zero-Shot Classifiers
items.headline: Logit-based label scoring on 11 open LLMs beats black-box confidence (AUROC 0.74-0.77 vs 0.57-0.66) and cuts decode steps 88-96%
items.summary: Compares ways to get calibrated confidence from LLMs used as zero-shot classifiers. Instead of generating a label and asking for confidence in text, it scores candidate labels directly from the model's logits. It studies 11 open-weight LLMs (1B-32B) on five classification datasets, and also examines the cost of single-token label IDs and decision-only scoring.
items.result: Logit-based scoring reaches AUROC 0.74-0.77 versus 0.57-0.66 for black-box methods. Single-token label IDs cost 3-6 accuracy points on average. Decision-only scoring reduces decode steps by 88-96% on the three largest label sets.
items.critique: Mostly a calibration study. The efficiency gain comes from skipping generation, which is expected. The method needs logit access, so closed API models are excluded. Five datasets only. Details rest on the arXiv listing abstract.

items.title: Learning to Read Events for Exact State Tracking with Frozen Language Models
items.headline: A selector on a frozen LM extracts events into an external integer register; concurrent extraction cuts median wall-clock 136.1 s to 10.4 s
items.summary: LLMs drift when they track state over very long event streams. This work trains a selector on top of a frozen language model to pull out individual event transitions, and delegates composition to an external integer register instead of the model's reasoning. Windows are extracted concurrently.
items.result: Concurrent extraction cut median wall-clock time from 136.1 to 10.4 s with Sonnet 5.5 and from 313.5 to 28.0 s with GPT-6.1 Sol. Mean cost per document fell 55% and 44%. A frozen 0.8B model read all 299 windows of 43,687 events each. A 27B model answered 3 of 100 two-event windows correctly without visible reasoning and 96 of 100 with intermediate steps.
items.critique: Single-author paper from a company (Attractor Dynamics Inc.). Speedups come mostly from parallelizing extraction rather than from a model change. The tasks are synthetic event logs. Cost figures assume fixed per-token prices. Details rest on the arXiv listing abstract.
